lesson.grammar_point: should and shouldn’t for advice, and the imperative for clear instructions

listenings.text: Hi, I'm Chris, and I manage a marketing team of six people in Chicago. When I started, I was a very nice boss. I never criticized anyone. It was a mistake. One day a person on my team made the same error for the third time, and I understood: nobody told him. Now I have a simple system. I have a one-on-one with each person every two weeks. I always start with something positive, and I'm specific. Then I say what can be better. My advice for new managers? You should give feedback soon, the same week. And you shouldn't give negative feedback by email. Talk to the person.

Hi, it's Priya. Two years ago I gave a presentation to our director. I thought it was great. After the meeting my manager asked me: do you have ten minutes? He took me to a small room, and he was very candid. He said: your data was excellent, but the presentation was too long, and the director stopped listening after ten minutes. You should start with the conclusion. I was a bit sad, but he was right, and he said it with care. He didn't say it in front of the team. Now, before every presentation, I think about his advice. Start with the conclusion. It changed my work.

paras: Radical Candor is a book about leadership by Kim Scott, a former manager at Google and Apple. Its main idea fits in one sentence: a good boss cares personally and challenges directly, at the same time. Most people think you have to choose: you are nice, or you are honest. Kim Scott says you should be both.

The book shows this with a simple square. When a manager cares but does not challenge, the result is ruinous empathy: the boss is nice, but the person never learns what is wrong. When a manager challenges but does not care, it is obnoxious aggression: the feedback is honest, but it hurts, and people lose trust. When a manager does neither, the book calls it manipulative insincerity. Radical candor is the fourth box: care and challenge together.

So what should a team lead do? Kim Scott gives practical advice. Praise in public, and criticize in private. Be specific: do not say good job, say exactly what was good. Give feedback soon, not three months later. And ask for feedback first: when a boss accepts criticism from the team, people feel safe to be candid and to push back.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- A2 summary of the main idea of Radical Candor, by Kim Scott (St. Martin’s Press, 2017)
